diagnostic_evidence.quote: we assume a noisy data set $\mathcal{D}_{\eta}$ obtained from corrupting the output $u$ by an additive Gaussian noise $\eta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma(a))$, i.e., $u_{\eta} = u + \eta$.
Suppose that the initial state $u_0$ follows a (nonzero mean) Gaussian distribution with the identity covariance, i.e., $u_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(m, \mathbf{I})$

issues.failure_explanation: The paper's general noisy data model allows arbitrary covariance $\Sigma(a)$. The justification for using $\Sigma_{\theta}(t,u_t,a)=\beta_t I$ in~\eqref{eqn:cov} relies on Proposition~\ref{prop:added-2}, which assumes $u_0 \sim N(m,I)$. For general $\Sigma(a)$, the true reverse covariance after integrating out $u_0$ depends on $\Sigma(a)$ and is not $\beta_t I$. Therefore, the claimed optimality does not hold for the stated general Gaussian noise setting.

failure_location.quote: Furthermore, after integrating out $u_0$ in~\eqref{eqn:true-reverse}, the true reverse distribution $p(u_{t-1} | u_t)$ has a covariance $\beta_t \mathbf{I}$. Hence, the parameterization~\eqref{eqn:cov} for $\Sigma_{\theta}$ in the Gaussian noise setting is optimal in the sense that $H_p(u_{t-1}|u_t) = H_{q_{\theta}}(u_{t-1}|u_t)$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either restrict the Gaussian noise model to identity covariance (or normalized data with unit noise variance) or derive the correct reverse covariance for general $\Sigma(a)$ and update~\eqref{eqn:cov}.
issues.overall_effect: The theoretical justification for the covariance choice in noisy data is invalid for arbitrary noise covariance; the claim that the method learns arbitrary $\Sigma(a)$ and recovers noise magnitude is unsupported.
issues.title: Gaussian-noise reverse covariance only justified for identity covariance
issues.why_classification: The defect affects the theoretical guarantee for arbitrary Gaussian noise, but a contained derivation or a limited restriction to normalized data can resolve it without invalidating the core method.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Since $q_{\theta}(u_T)$ is assumed to be a standard Gaussian

issues.failure_explanation: For noise-free data $u_0$ is deterministic. Then $p(u_T|u_0)$ has covariance $(1-\bar{\alpha}_T)I$, so $H_p(u_T) \neq H_{q_{\theta}}(u_T)$ unless $\bar{\alpha}_T=0$. The paper itself states $u_T$ is only approximately standard normal for large $T$. Thus the exact equality is false for finite $T$.

failure_location.quote:
In both cases, the noise-free and Gaussian noise, the learned parametric model $q_{\theta}$ achieves the exact likelihood under the true model $p$, i.e., 
\[
\mathbb{E}_{q_{\theta}}\left[-\log q_{\theta}(u_{0:T}) \right]
=
H_{q_{\theta}}(u_T) + \sum_{t=1}^T H_{q_{\theta}}(u_{t-1} | u_t) 
=
H_p(u_T) + \sum_{t=1}^T H_p(u_{t-1} | u_t) 
=
\mathbb{E}_{p}\left[-\log p(u_{0:T}) \right].
\]

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the exact equality with an approximate equality (or take $T\to\infty$) and clarify that the likelihood is exact only in the limit.
issues.overall_effect: The claim that the model achieves exact likelihood in the noise-free case is unsupported; only an approximate statement holds.
issues.title: Exact likelihood claim ignores non-standard $u_T$ in noise-free case
issues.why_classification: The error is a local overstatement in an appendix justification; the algorithm and main empirical results do not depend on exactness for finite $T$.
